dossier.deep_context:
# 1768 in 2026: the rebuild is a sequence of decisions, not one drum photograph

This supplement uses the team’s October CAD-release replies alongside the earlier technical interview. It distinguishes the original Nightshade, the Nightshift rebuild, later onseason adjustments and offseason changes. The source is unusually useful because the team explains why mechanisms and schedule choices were coupled. A successful rebuild should not be reduced to “replace two shooters with a drum,” nor should October performance be assigned to the robot that competed at Worlds.

## The schedule establishes what the team actually proved

The team describes an eleven-day rebuild between URI in week 3 and WPI in week 5, with the new machine operational after nine days. Only the swerve modules and bellypan were retained. The reply’s timeline runs from the original robot’s final match on March 21 through CAD on March 25, stripping the old machine on March 27, mounting major subsystems on March 28 and reaching a practice field on April 2. Those are dated milestones reported by the team, not an inference that another team can repeat the schedule. [Schedule and retained hardware](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/12). [Detailed milestones](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/13).

The distinction matters when borrowing architecture. A mechanism whose drawings can be completed quickly may still consume the entire available interval in wiring, controls, feeding tests and driver learning. Conversely, retaining a technically mediocre but known assembly can preserve enough practice time to win more matches. The relevant rebuild calculation includes the probability of arriving with an integrated machine, not just the predicted performance of the finished CAD. An architecture recommendation should name the existing interfaces that survive, the ones that are replaced and the latest date at which a failed experiment can still be abandoned.

The team’s process reply describes student ownership of deadlines and explicit gates: if a new assembly does not meet a milestone, the original version stays. Older students handled CAD while newer students manufactured early enough to understand assembly. This is evidence about the organization that made a rapid rebuild possible. It is not a universal staffing prescription. [Process account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/21).

For a PCH rebuild, the transferable question is therefore not “can our team also rebuild in eleven days?” It is “which uncertainty can our actual team retire before our next event, with enough time left to integrate and practice?” A new hopper that retains the old collector, floor and mounting interfaces can be a fundamentally different risk from a new collector, hopper and feed path that must all work on their first combined test. The latter may still be justified, but the justification needs an integration plan and a fallback with a real deadline.

## The four-bar is doing more than deploying an intake

The later replies explain that the week-zero machine did not stow under the trench. On the developed machine, the hopper attaches to the lower link of the four-bar. The team describes fitting the trench envelope in both positions, satisfying the starting envelope, folding the kicker and choosing link angles that survive contact. They arrived at the geometry through iteration rather than a single independent constraint calculation. [Envelope discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/15). [Coupled geometry](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/16).

This is exactly why “a 2910-style intake with a Citrus hopper” needs an interface analysis. The intake’s ground contact point and deployed reach are only part of the design. The moving hopper wall changes where stored fuel rests; the lower link’s motion changes the floor slope; the kicker’s folded position changes what can occupy the trench envelope. The mechanism must pass through intermediate positions while full of fuel. A configuration that clears a field element in a static CAD screenshot can still trap fuel, pull a flexible wall into a roller or require a transition that cannot be completed while moving.

The useful inspiration is the constraint-solving strategy: let one linkage carry several compatible motions, then check the consequences as a system. It is not a claim that the same link lengths fit another chassis. A receiving team should record the deployed and retracted volumes, the swept paths of rigid members and flexible walls, the lowest loaded floor point, the expected collision direction and the fuel escape routes. If any of those are unknown, the recommendation should remain an architectural candidate rather than a dimensioned solution.

## Transmission failures need local explanations

One reply separates motor-to-roller belt skipping from roller-to-roller belts that did not skip. The team changed the former to chain after Worlds, then added polycarbonate retaining flanges after the chain came off once. Their explanation involves possible motor or plate flex reducing wrap or tension around a small pulley; it is a team hypothesis about this installation. [Transmission sequence](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/9).

That report does not establish “chain is better than belts.” It suggests tests: watch relative motor and shaft displacement under load; inspect tooth engagement through the entire torque transient; distinguish a belt climbing out of mesh from a shaft or tensioner moving; and check retention after changing the transmission type. A mechanism database should keep the failed condition, the suspected cause, the modification and the observed result as separate fields. Without that separation, an agent may copy the final component while repeating the geometry that caused the original failure.

The sliding flywheel-belt tensioner belongs to an offseason N.E.R.D. update. The team reports that high-speed slack had been damaging the belt, that the tensioner improved reported accuracy and that short testing had not yet revealed issues. They also anticipated possible creep that could be corrected by retensioning. Another reply explains the generous adjustment range and the washer arrangement around the bearing. [Tensioner report](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/8). [Adjustment explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/11). This is promising design evidence with a limited test horizon, not a season-long reliability certification.

## Fabrication and service choices change what is feasible

The team explains choosing live axles because they were quickest to manufacture for this rebuild. They recognize advantages of stubs for width iteration, but that was not the priority. This is a concrete example of a choice that can be strategically correct despite not maximizing every engineering objective. [Axle tradeoff](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/12).

Their hood-rack reply describes printed material supported by aluminum teeth, with print settings chosen to reduce backlash. The lesson is to document the load path and what each material contributes. A screenshot that looks like a printed rack can conceal metal reinforcement; a recommendation to “print the rack” can therefore remove the part that made it survive. [Rack construction](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/17).

## Do not backdate the faster feeder

October replies describe an entry roller using spaced compliant wheels to create lanes, combining the entry roller and floor drive at a 1:1 ratio, and matching feeder surface speed more closely to drum speed. The team reports moving from roughly 23–26 to 28–30 balls per second. These are offseason reports, not measured Worlds match averages. [October feed changes](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/22). [Reported result](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/24).

The architectural implication is broader than the headline firing rate. Fuel must arrive across the useful shooter width with suitable velocity, spacing and compression. Adding lanes can change the stability of that delivery; linking drives can remove one mismatch while introducing another dependency. A team evaluating the change should compare the beginning and end of a full hopper, partly depleted operation, worn fuel, lateral acceleration and recovery after a jam. A clean burst of a few fuel does not test those conditions.

## What an agent should retrieve from this case

Retrieve 1768 when the question involves a compressed rebuild, a moving hopper carried by a four-bar, drum packaging or separating onseason and offseason transmission fixes. Pair it with 254 and 1678 for feed-contact geometry and with 2910 for a different rebuild triggered by unmet performance goals. Do not merge the named configurations into a single idealized robot. The strongest reusable lesson is that an architecture is a set of coordinated constraints, a manufacturing plan and a validated operating sequence. The remaining unresolved endgame and exact drivetrain details in the base dossier remain unresolved; these additional replies do not establish them.

context_documents.title: 2026-1768 · Rebuild removes feed compression and separates shooter readiness
context_documents.body:
# 2026-1768: Rebuild removes feed compression and separates shooter readiness

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The interview distinguishes a former divided two-lane/double-spindexer arrangement from the drum rebuild with a roller floor. A powered lower intake roller was replaced by two 3/4-inch aluminum shafts with reduced compression. Compliant wheels near entry feed a J-shaped path; a guide was added after WPI wobble. Four motors drive the drum/kicker/hood group, and feed is enabled only after aiming, speed and hood conditions are satisfied.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team reports improved throughput after reducing collector compression, adds the guide to control observed motion, and describes reduced belt tension as a current-draw improvement. Driver controls were intentionally simplified around repeatable actions.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

This is evidence against treating maximum grip as maximum throughput. Too many opposing powered contacts can trap deformable fuel or make its entry velocity inconsistent. Removing a roller changes the entire force chain, so the improvement should not be generalized to a collector with different ground geometry. Likewise, the software shoot command is a sequencer rather than a simultaneous motor-on command. Feeding early can pull down wheel speed or create an inaccurate initial volley, while waiting unnecessarily long reduces usable shift time.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Compare feed latency, initial-volley accuracy, current and residual fuel with the actual readiness tolerances. Inspect the added guide over hood travel and repeat reduced-compression tests with worn fuel.

## Limits

Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

## Sources and navigation

- [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zxBvVSZtS3E](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zxBvVSZtS3E)
- [https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192)

source_reviews.title: Nashoba Robotics Nightshift reveal
source_reviews.review_basis: Read April release and the Nightshade follow-up.
source_reviews.facts: Nightshift used four X60 drum motors and an independently driven shooter entry roller. The earlier twin indexer required local field tuning at URI.
source_reviews.limitations: Reveal supplies an onseason anchor, with few dimensions and no event-by-event build list.

source_reviews.title: Team 1768 2026 release and retrospective
source_reviews.review_basis: Read team's schedule, failure reports, gearing changes and results in the public thread.
source_reviews.facts: Only swerves and bellypan survived rebuild as original components. A motor-to-entry pinch affected the old machine. Offseason changes coupled floor, entry and shooter gearing.
source_reviews.limitations: Reported BPS and accuracy are team estimates without a shared test protocol.

source_reviews.title: Nashoba Robotics Tech Slides
source_reviews.review_basis: Downloaded team attachment and read the extracted mechanism specifications.
source_reviews.facts: Slides give intake, linkage, hopper, floor and drum construction and ratios. They include changes the team separately dates to offseason.
source_reviews.limitations: The slides and post 16 describe the moving hopper attachment differently. Verify the actual link and hardware version before transferring dimensions.

source_review.whole_robot_explanation: Nightshade used divided shooting and twin spindexer feed. Nightshift changed the central fuel path to a full-width roller floor, shooter entry and drum while retaining much of the intake concept. The team reports nine days to operational status within the eleven-day gap from URI to WPI. The bellypan and swerve modules were the physical carryovers. Later offseason changes shifted the limiting interface again, from floor supply to launch consistency and battery sag.
source_review.piece_flow: Nightshade needed fuel to drop into space between the battery and omni wheel while avoiding the counterrotating-wheel region. Fuel caught between a Kraken and the entry roller could stop the system. Nightshift feeds from an expanding hopper over a broad roller floor, through the compliant entry and into the drum and powered hood rollers. The spaced entry wheels introduced before IRI were intended to organize lanes and reduce lateral interactions between launched fuel.
source_review.packaging_and_motion: Four-bar stow couples bumper clearance, hopper movement and trench height. Week 0 did not fit stowed. Later geometry allowed a trench start aimed toward midfield and folded the kicker over the bumper. The slides describe a bumper-mounted stationary hopper and a moving section with SRPP sides, polycarbonate back, carbon tube and freely rotating sleeves to reduce trapped fuel.

subsystems.name: Four-bar intake and expandable hopper
subsystems.construction: Two two-inch polycarbonate rollers with silicone grip, static half-hex kicker bars, SRPP upper links, aluminum lower links and a MaxSpline jackshaft under the floor. Slides describe one X60 at 90:1 deploy reduction.
subsystems.operation: Cross-shaft and chains drive both sides. The lower links provide a repeatable hard stop and the hopper changes volume with deployment.
subsystems.team_rationale: Team optimized trench clearance while keeping the intake inside perimeter at start and leaving useful internal space.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Flexible plates that survive impact may still move transmission centers enough to lose tooth engagement. A rigid load path across the transmission can be sized separately from the rest of the side plate.
subsystems.interfaces: Deploy shaft to links, kicker to bumper, moving wall to collector, roller motor to first roller.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: After Worlds a chain replaced a skipping motor belt. A thrown chain prompted polycarbonate flanges. Team suspected plate flex and poor wrap on a 12-tooth pulley. Roller-to-roller belt had no reported skipping.
subsystems.unknowns: Resolve upper-versus-lower hopper attachment wording by build version and measure belt-center displacement under torque.

subsystems.name: Floor and entry
subsystems.construction: WCP stubs and custom plugs, three through-shafts of squish wheels, thin aluminum tube rollers with silicone, and shortened belt center distances by 0.030 inch. April entry had its own X60.
subsystems.operation: Floor conveys fuel toward the entry. Offseason revisions combined floor and entry drives, then increased floor speed as launch consistency improved.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team shortened centers to reduce current and tried spaced entry wheels to separate fuel into lanes.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Speed increases shift load downstream. Compare full-width trajectories before increasing floor command, and log chain motion as well as average current.
subsystems.interfaces: Hopper to floor, floor rollers to compliant entry, entry to drum compression zone.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: The combined chain could contact itself in long operation. Confirm chain clearance with warmed hardware and accumulated slack.
subsystems.unknowns: Loaded current by version and whether all lanes feed equally at low fill.

subsystems.name: Drum and hood
subsystems.construction: Four X60s drive a four-inch aluminum drum with CatTongue tape. Slides specify powered hood rollers, a roughly three-pound external steel flywheel, and a 20-DP printed hood rack flanked by aluminum plates.
subsystems.operation: The hood pivots under X44 power. A later ratio brought kicker surface speed closer to the drum. Team reports spinning up from zero for each shot.
subsystems.team_rationale: Flanking rack plates resist tooth shear. The team matched surfaces more closely to improve shot consistency and regarded continuous spin as poor value given inertia and kicker friction.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Reducing surface speed mismatch can narrow launch variation, but fast feed and a lower-angle, higher-power shot can erode voltage headroom.
subsystems.interfaces: Entry release to drum, drum to hood contact, rack mesh to hood position, shared electrical supply to drivetrain.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Offseason flywheel belt slack caused shredding and led to a sliding tensioner. Team reports late-match brownouts after faster tuning.
subsystems.unknowns: Onseason exit-speed distribution, power traces, hood angle map and initial versus final flywheel ratios.

revisions: Nightshade used improvised Lexan, cardboard and tape guides. Nightshift rebuilt after Week 3, with later DCMP intake work. Before IRI came spaced entry wheels, then combined floor and entry and revised shooter gearing. Team ultimately reported about 28 BPS at RiverRage.
transferable_principles: Treat a rebuild as an interface and schedule decision. Separate drop-in space, transport rate and shot quality in validation. Leave time for code changes when mechanisms become mechanically coupled.
disconfirming_conditions: More feed is counterproductive if trajectory spread or brownout reduces total makes. A similar four-bar loses value if local frame and bumper geometry cannot accommodate the required trench states.
remaining_gaps: Endgame installation, final swerve spec, tested current and precise event chronology for every intake detail remain open.
